examples.name: Java Cloneable / Object.clone()
examples.note: Object.clone() is a protected native method that produces a field-by-field shallow copy; a class must implement the Cloneable marker interface or the call throws CloneNotSupportedException. Deep copies require overriding clone() to duplicate nested mutable state by hand, since the default only copies references.

examples.name: Python copy module

A class customises either by implementing __copy__ or __deepcopy__ (the latter receives the memo).

examples.name: Rust Clone trait
examples.note: Types implement Clone (usually via #[derive(Clone)], which requires every field to be Clone) so .clone() yields an explicit, independent duplicate. It is distinct from Copy: Clone is always an explicit call and may be arbitrarily deep, whereas Copy is an implicit bitwise duplication for trivial values.

examples.name: The DOM
examples.note: Every node — element, text, comment — exposes the same Node interface with childNodes, appendChild, and removeChild; a leaf text node still has appendChild, it just throws HierarchyRequestError, making the DOM the textbook transparent composite. Whole-subtree operations like cloneNode(true) and textContent recurse without the caller ever managing the descent.

examples.name: Java Swing / AWT Container
examples.note: java.awt.Container extends Component yet holds a list of child Components, so a panel of nested panels sits in the same tree as a lone button. Painting, validation, and layout all recurse through the hierarchy — validate() walks the subtree and each container delegates the positioning of its own children to its LayoutManager.

examples.name: Java String pool
examples.note: String literals are interned automatically at class load and String.intern() adds a runtime string, returning one canonical instance per distinct value; the pool is a fixed-capacity hash table whose bucket count is tunable via -XX:StringTableSize.

examples.note: Returns cached shared Integer instances for values in the range -128..127, so autoboxing there reuses objects rather than allocating; the upper bound is tunable via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax (java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high).

examples.name: Python sys.intern
examples.note: Stores one shared copy of a str in the interpreter intern table so repeated identical values point at the same object; CPython auto-interns identifier-like literals, and manual interning speeds dict lookups and identity (is) comparisons.

examples.name: gRPC client stubs
examples.note: The generated blocking or async stub implements the service interface locally, marshals each call to protobuf and ships it over HTTP/2 to the remote server, unmarshaling the reply so callers invoke a remote method as if it were local.

examples.name: JavaScript Proxy
examples.note: The built-in Proxy wraps a target with a handler whose traps (get, set, has, apply, deleteProperty) intercept the matching operations while presenting the target shape; Vue 3 reactivity uses it to track property reads and writes.

examples.name: Express.js middleware
examples.note: Functions with the (req, res, next) signature run in registration order; each either ends the cycle by sending a response or calls next() to pass control on. Calling next(err) skips straight to the error-handling middleware, distinguished by its four-argument (err, req, res, next) signature.

examples.name: Java Servlet Filters
examples.note: Each filter doFilter(request, response, chain) does its work then calls chain.doFilter() to reach the next filter; skipping that call short-circuits the request. Order comes from web.xml filter-mapping declarations or the @WebFilter annotation, and the same chain wraps the response on the way back out.

examples.name: ASP.NET Core middleware
examples.note: The pipeline is built in Program.cs from app.Use(...) components that receive a next delegate and decide whether to invoke it; app.Run(...) is terminal and never calls next. Registration order is execution order, and each component can run code both before and after awaiting the rest of the pipeline.

examples.note: An Action extends ActionListener with bound state: an enabled flag, name, icon, and accelerator key. One instance shared by a toolbar button, a menu item, and a key binding keeps them all enabled or disabled together when setEnabled() is called.

Expressions parse to a protobuf AST that can be type-checked against a declared environment before running against a runtime activation.

examples.name: java.util.Iterator

examples.name: Python generators
examples.note: A function containing yield returns a generator implementing __iter__/__next__; each next() runs to the following yield and suspends, so elements are produced lazily. next() raises StopIteration at the end, and close() releases resources held open across yields.

examples.name: JavaScript Symbol.iterator
examples.note: An object is iterable if it has a [Symbol.iterator]() method returning an object whose next() yields {value, done}. That contract powers for...of, spread, and destructuring; generator functions (function*) produce it automatically.

examples.name: ZFS snapshots
examples.note: A snapshot records a read-only, point-in-time image of a dataset, and a later rollback returns that dataset to exactly the recorded state. Snapshots are cheap enough to keep in sequence, which makes expiry policy — deciding which old ones to drop — a standing concern.

examples.name: Virtual machine snapshots
examples.note: Hypervisors such as VMware and VirtualBox capture the state of a virtual machine — disk contents, and memory and device state when it is running — as a named snapshot, then revert the machine to that exact point on request. examples.name: CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace)

examples.name: opossum
examples.note: The Node circuit breaker: wrap an async function and it trips on errorThresholdPercentage (50 by default) measured over a rollingCountTimeout window split into rollingCountBuckets, holds open for resetTimeout (30 s) then goes half-open, and counts a call that exceeds timeout (10 s) as a failure. A volumeThreshold keeps a quiet endpoint from tripping on one error, .fallback() supplies the degraded path, and open, halfOpen and close are events you can export as metrics.

examples.name: AWS Step Functions + DynamoDB
examples.note: AWS documents the breaker as shared state rather than a per-process counter: a workflow reads a CircuitStatus table before calling, fails fast if an unexpired record exists for that callee, and writes one with an expiry timestamp after the retries are exhausted. DynamoDB TTL deletes the expired records, so the breaker closes itself with no sweeper — and every replica sees the same state.

examples.name: Netflix Hystrix
examples.note: Popularized the pattern in the JVM world: trips on an error percentage over a rolling window once a minimum request volume is met (errorThresholdPercentage, requestVolumeThreshold), then waits a sleep window before probing. Now in maintenance mode, with Resilience4j the usual successor.

examples.name: Envoy
examples.note: Outlier detection ejects an upstream host after consecutive 5xx or gateway failures, holds it out for a base ejection time that grows with repeat ejections, then probes it back in — with max_ejection_percent capping how much of the pool can be removed at once.

examples.name: Polly
examples.note: The .NET resilience library; its circuit-breaker strategy trips on a failure ratio measured over a sampling duration above a minimum throughput, and composes in a pipeline with retry and timeout.

examples.name: AWS SDK
examples.note: The retry curve is configuration, not code: retry_mode picks standard, the default, which retries transient and throttling errors with exponential backoff and jitter bounded by max_attempts (3 by default). Its retry quota is a token bucket charged per retry and refunded on success, so sustained failure drains it and the client fails fast instead of adding load to a service already struggling. Adaptive mode adds a client-side rate limiter that can delay even the initial request once the service signals throttling — useful against one hot resource, harmful on a client that fans out across many.

examples.name: p-retry
examples.note: The Node wrapper for the same curve as options rather than a loop: retries (10 by default), factor (2), minTimeout (1 s), maxTimeout (unbounded) and randomize for jitter. A shouldRetry predicate and an AbortError stop the loop immediately on an error that will never succeed — the non-transient case backoff must never paper over.

examples.name: gRPC
examples.note: Service config declares a retryPolicy with maxAttempts, initialBackoff, maxBackoff, backoffMultiplier, and the set of retryable status codes, applied by the client library — plus channel-level retry throttling (a token bucket) that disables retries when failures dominate, guarding against storms.

examples.name: Kubernetes

examples.name: Apache Flink

examples.name: HTCondor
examples.note: A scheduler built for large numbers of independent tasks rather than one coupled job. It will run work opportunistically on machines that are otherwise idle and reschedule a task when its machine is reclaimed, which only works because each task is repeatable.

examples.name: BOINC and Folding@home
examples.note: Volunteer computing taken to its limit: independent tasks are shipped to donated machines across the internet, results come back over ordinary networking, and a contributor who disappears mid-task costs one requeue. examples.name: Amazon SQS
examples.note: The canonical buffer in front of workers: producers enqueue and return while consumers drain at their own rate. A VisibilityTimeout hides an in-flight message during processing, and a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount routes repeat failures to a dead-letter queue; standard queues are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

examples.name: Apache Kafka
examples.note: A durable, replayable partitioned log absorbs ingestion bursts while a consumer group reads at its own pace. Offsets track progress and enable replay, retention (by time or size) bounds how long messages persist, and consumer lag — log-end offset minus committed offset — is the backlog measure.

examples.name: Celery
examples.note: A Python web request hands a task to a broker (Redis or RabbitMQ) and responds immediately; worker processes pick it up later. Workers prefetch tasks by a configurable multiplier, acks_late redelivers a task if the worker crashes mid-run, and time limits bound how long any one task may run.

examples.name: PostgreSQL WAL
examples.note: Every change is written to the WAL and fsynced before the heap page is touched; the same log (default 16 MB segments) drives streaming replication and point-in-time recovery. synchronous_commit tunes the durability/latency tradeoff, and checkpoint_timeout with max_wal_size governs how far recovery ever replays.

examples.name: SQLite WAL mode
examples.note: journal_mode=WAL sends changes to a separate -wal file with a shared-memory index (-shm), so readers keep reading a consistent snapshot of the main database while a writer appends. A checkpoint (auto-triggered around 1000 pages by default, or PRAGMA wal_checkpoint) folds the log back into the db file.

examples.name: MySQL InnoDB redo log
examples.note: Commits land in the redo log first; dirty buffer-pool pages are flushed lazily and replayed from the log after a crash. innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit picks whether every commit fsyncs (1, fully durable) or batches flushes for throughput (0 or 2).

examples.name: RocksDB
examples.note: Writes hit the WAL before the in-memory memtable, so an unflushed memtable is rebuildable after a restart. Once a memtable is flushed to an SST file its WAL segment can be discarded, and WriteOptions.sync chooses per-write whether the append is fsynced.

examples.name: Amazon S3 lifecycle rules

examples.name: Apache Kafka
examples.note: Publishers append to a partitioned topic; each consumer group tracks its own offset, so groups read independently and can replay. Retention is bounded by retention.ms or retention.bytes, and ordering holds within a partition, not across the topic.

examples.name: MQTT
examples.note: A lightweight pub/sub protocol for IoT: subscribers match topic filters with the + and # wildcards, three QoS levels trade delivery guarantee for overhead, and a retained message gives a new subscriber the last value on a topic immediately.

examples.name: Google Cloud Pub/Sub
examples.note: Publishers write to a topic and each subscription gets an independent copy of the stream; a per-message ackDeadline governs redelivery, unacked messages are retained up to the configured window, and a dead-letter topic catches messages that exceed a max delivery attempts.

examples.name: Amazon SNS
examples.note: A fully managed pub/sub service: publish to a topic and SNS pushes each message to every subscription — SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP/S endpoints, email; per-subscription filter policies match message attributes so a subscriber only receives matching messages, and undeliverable messages go to a redrive dead-letter queue. Standard topics take unlimited messages per second with best-effort ordering and deduplication; FIFO topics trade that throughput for strict ordering and deduplication, at up to 300 messages or 10 MB per second per topic.

examples.name: Amazon EventBridge
examples.note: The routing-heavy end of the same idea: producers put events on a bus and subscribers are rules rather than subscriptions, matching on the content of the event and fanning each match out to its own targets. It buys content-based routing and filtering across producers that speak different shapes, at the cost of the wiring living in rule definitions rather than in either side's code.

examples.name: Single-threaded command execution
examples.note: A store that runs every command on one thread confines all of its state to that thread: because only one thread ever mutates the data, there are no locks and no data races by construction. Concurrency comes from non-blocking I/O around the loop, not from multiple threads on the data — the classic single-threaded event-loop store design.

examples.name: Java ThreadLocal

examples.name: Kafka consumer groups

examples.name: Sidekiq
examples.note: Ruby workers compete for jobs on shared Redis queues, each process running a pool of threads (concurrency) that pull with BRPOP. examples.name: Amazon SQS

examples.name: Linux fork()

Forking a large process is therefore cheap until one side starts writing.

examples.name: ZFS and Btrfs

examples.name: OpenBSD pledge
examples.note: A process calls pledge(2) to voluntarily restrict itself to a named set of promises (stdio, rpath, inet, ...); once pledged it cannot widen the set, and a call outside the set usually aborts the process with SIGABRT. Pledging the error promise instead makes most violating calls fail with ENOSYS, so the process can handle the refusal rather than die. Its companion unveil(2) does the same for filesystem paths.

examples.name: Linux capabilities
examples.note: The monolithic power of root is split into discrete units (capabilities(7)); a process granted only CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE can bind a port below 1024 without holding any other superuser power, so a daemon runs with a fraction of full privilege.

examples.name: AWS STS temporary credentials
examples.note: AssumeRole mints short-lived credentials with an explicit session duration (DurationSeconds, from 15 minutes up to 12 hours) in place of long-lived access keys, and an inline session policy can further narrow the assumed role to only what the current task needs.

examples.name: NGINX

examples.name: Argo Rollouts
examples.note: Its BlueGreen strategy keeps an activeService and a previewService pointing at two ReplicaSets, promotes by re-pointing the active service, and holds the old ReplicaSet for a configurable scaleDownDelaySeconds so a rollback needs no rebuild.

examples.name: AWS CodeDeploy blue/green
examples.note: CodeDeploy provisions a replacement set of instances or tasks, registers them behind a second load balancer target group, shifts traffic to it, and can roll back by shifting the listener back to the original group.

examples.name: Azure App Service deployment slots
examples.note: A staging slot runs the new version on its own worker, is warmed up before the swap, and the swap exchanges the routing of the two slots — so swapping back is the documented rollback.

fault-injection.name: Fault Injection
fault-injection.essence: Break it on purpose, on a schedule, to prove it survives
solves: we think the system survives a dependency going down but nobody has ever checked
the failure path has never run outside a design document
our timeouts and retry settings were copied from another service and nobody knows if they fit
the mechanism worked during the incident and nobody was alerted
we promise an availability number and have no evidence for it

relations.note: Injecting a failing dependency is how you find out the breaker actually trips
relations.name: Circuit Breaker
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Saturating one compartment proves the others were really isolated
relations.name: Bulkhead
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Returning errors on purpose exposes a retry with no ceiling or no jitter
relations.name: Retry with Backoff
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Added latency is the fastest way to find a missing or over-generous timeout
relations.name: Timeout / Deadline
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The experiment checks whether the probe noticed, not just whether the code coped
relations.name: Health Endpoint Monitoring
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Rehearse the first failure and find the spread before it happens for real
relations.name: Cascading Failure
relations.label: Prevents

relations.note: A deliberate outage under load makes the amplification visible in a controlled window
relations.name: Retry Storm
relations.label: Prevents

themes.name: Continuous Validation
themes.role: Check the safeguards still work

examples.name: Netflix Chaos Monkey
examples.note: The tool that named the practice: it terminates instances at random during working hours, which enforces one property continuously — nothing may depend on a particular instance staying alive.

examples.name: AWS Fault Injection Service
examples.note: Runs experiment templates that inject faults such as instance termination, added API latency and resource exhaustion, with stop conditions bound to CloudWatch alarms so the experiment aborts itself when a metric leaves its bounds.

examples.name: Azure Chaos Studio
examples.note: Runs fault experiments against Azure resources as a pipeline step, which is how the mission-critical reference architecture validates resiliency: chaos experiments execute alongside a load test so the injected fault lands on a system that is actually under pressure.

canary-release.name: Canary Release
canary-release.essence: Send a small slice of traffic to the new version and watch before widening
solves: a release passed every test and still broke in production
we only find out a deploy was bad when every user is already on it
there is no way to try a change against real traffic without exposing everyone
our error rate went up after a deploy and we cannot tell if it is the deploy or the day
rolling back means all users had the bad version first

relations.note: Ramp the release with the router, one feature with a flag
relations.name: Feature Flag
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A candidate that reports unhealthy leaves rotation before the gate runs
relations.name: Health Endpoint Monitoring
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The slice can be a whole stamp rather than a percentage
relations.name: Deployment Stamp
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Pairs with a supply-chain gate: check what you ship, then who sees it first
relations.name: Quarantine
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Ramp gradually, or flip everyone across in one routing change
relations.name: Blue-Green Deployment
relations.label: Alternative to

relations.name: Load Balancer
relations.label: Requires

examples.name: Argo Rollouts
examples.note: Its canary strategy is a list of steps — setWeight and pause — and an AnalysisTemplate that queries a metrics provider between steps, promoting or aborting the rollout on the query result rather than on a human watching a dashboard.

examples.name: Flagger
examples.note: A Kubernetes operator that drives progressive delivery on top of a service mesh or ingress controller: it steps the traffic weight up on a schedule, runs metric checks and webhooks at each step, and rolls back automatically when a check fails.

examples.name: Istio
examples.note: A VirtualRoute splits traffic across subsets by weight, which is the routing primitive a canary needs; the mesh also emits per-subset request metrics, so the candidate and the baseline are measurable without changing the application.

distributed-tracing.name: Distributed Tracing
distributed-tracing.essence: Follow one request across every service it touches, as a single timeline
solves: a page is slow and six services each say they were fast
we cannot tell which service the error actually started in
correlating log files by timestamp across services is how every incident begins
nobody knows the real call graph any more, only the one on the diagram
the p99 spiked and we have no example of a request that was slow

relations.note: The same idea inside a message flow: a shared id is what lets separate records be reassembled into one story
relations.name: Correlation Identifier
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The mesh proxy can start and propagate spans on every hop without any application change
relations.name: Service Mesh
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Exporting spans from a companion process keeps the tracing SDK and its configuration out of the application
relations.name: Sidecar
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A probe says whether an instance is healthy; a trace says which hop made a request slow
relations.name: Health Endpoint Monitoring
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Without it, a fully decoupled multi-region topology is effectively opaque
relations.name: Geode
relations.label: Combines with

themes.name: Observability
themes.role: Reassemble one request into a single timeline

themes.name: Health Modeling
themes.role: Explain the verdict once it turns

examples.name: OpenTelemetry
examples.note: The CNCF project that standardises the API, the SDKs and the wire protocol for traces, metrics and logs, plus a vendor-neutral collector. It is what lets instrumentation be written once and pointed at a different backend later.

examples.name: W3C Trace Context
examples.note: The recommendation that defines the traceparent and tracestate headers. Being a published standard rather than a vendor format is exactly why two independently built services can join one trace.

examples.name: Jaeger
examples.note: A CNCF distributed tracing backend that collects, stores and queries spans, with support for sampling decided centrally rather than hardcoded in each service.

examples.name: Google Dapper
examples.note: The 2010 paper describing the internal tracing system that established the model — trace ids, spans, parent links, and low sampling rates as the way to make it affordable. Nearly every system since follows its shape.

feature-flag.name: Feature Flag
feature-flag.essence: Ship the code dark, then turn the behaviour on separately
solves: turning a broken feature off means waiting for another build
unfinished work sits on a branch for weeks and the merge is a nightmare
we cannot let a few customers try something without shipping it to everyone
product wants to launch on a date and engineering wants to ship when it is ready
an expensive optional feature is dragging the whole service down under load

relations.note: A percentage rule ramps one behaviour without a new deployment
relations.name: Canary Release
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The flag is the switch that sends a slice to the replacement
relations.name: Strangler Fig
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A kill switch sheds an expensive path deliberately, before the server has to
relations.name: Load Shedding
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A runtime switch between two paths, chosen by configuration rather than by type
relations.name: Strategy
relations.label: Alternative to

relations.note: Where flags live once more than one instance has to agree on them
relations.name: External Configuration Store
relations.label: Requires

themes.name: Continuous Validation
themes.role: Validate one behaviour without a release

themes.name: Operating a Live System
themes.role: Change behaviour in seconds, without a build

examples.name: OpenFeature
examples.note: A CNCF specification and set of SDKs that put a vendor-neutral evaluation API in front of whichever flag backend you use, so the branch points in the code do not have to be rewritten when the provider changes.

examples.name: LaunchDarkly
examples.note: A hosted flag service whose SDKs stream rule updates into an in-process store, so evaluation happens locally against cached rules rather than as a network call on each request.

examples.name: Unleash
examples.note: An open-source flag service built around activation strategies — gradual rollout, user lists, and similar rules — evaluated by the client SDK from a periodically fetched rule set.

pagination.name: Pagination
pagination.essence: Hand back a large collection in bounded slices the caller asks for one at a time
solves: a list endpoint times out because the table grew past a million rows
the export job re-reads the same record and misses another one entirely
page 900 of the search results takes twelve seconds and page 1 takes forty milliseconds
one client asked for limit=100000 and took the database down
the total count on the results page costs more than the results

relations.note: The page-size cap belongs at the front door, where it is enforced before a request reaches your handler
relations.name: API Gateway
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A page cap bounds one request; a rate limit bounds the sequence of them, and a walk needs both
relations.name: Rate Limiter
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Paging a collection spread over shards means a page from each shard and a merge before the answer
relations.name: Scatter-Gather
relations.label: Combines with

themes.name: API Design
themes.role: Bound what one request can return, however much data exists

examples.name: Stripe API
examples.note: Cursor pagination across every list endpoint: limit bounds the page, starting_after and ending_before carry an object id rather than an offset, and has_more tells the caller whether to continue. No total count is returned.

examples.name: GitHub REST API
examples.note: Offset paging with page and per_page, and the next page advertised in a Link header with rel="next", rel="prev" and rel="last" — so a client follows links instead of computing offsets.

examples.name: Elasticsearch
examples.note: Deep paging is capped rather than merely discouraged: from plus size may not exceed index.max_result_window, which defaults to 10,000. Past that you use search_after, pinned to a point-in-time so the traversal reads one consistent view.

examples.name: Kubernetes API
examples.note: List requests take a limit and return a continue token that the next request echoes back — an opaque cursor whose encoding the API server is free to change.

api-versioning.name: API Versioning
api-versioning.essence: Change a published contract while the callers built on the old one keep working
solves: I need to rename a field but partner integrations read it by name
we cannot ship the fix because we do not control the apps that call us
every release breaks somebody and we find out from their support ticket
we have five versions live and nobody knows who is still on the oldest
the proxy served a client the wrong shape of response and we cannot reproduce it

relations.note: A path segment or a header is what routing dispatches on, so the version reaches the right handler
relations.name: API Routing
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A translation layer per published version keeps the domain model single while the contracts differ
relations.name: Anti-Corruption Layer
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The payload shape is what a version actually versions, so the transfer object is where a version lives
relations.name: DTO
relations.label: Combines with

themes.name: API Design
themes.role: Change the contract without a release from callers you do not control

themes.name: Microservices Design
themes.role: Ship a change without breaking callers you do not control

themes.name: Continuous Delivery
themes.role: Ship a breaking change without breaking clients

examples.name: Kubernetes API
examples.note: The version is a path segment beside the API group — /apis/apps/v1 — and carries a maturity level in its name (alpha, beta, stable) that tells callers what stability to expect. Objects are stored in one version and converted on the way out, which is the translation-layer approach made explicit.

examples.name: Stripe API
examples.note: Versions are dates rather than integers, pinned per account and overridable per request with the Stripe-Version header. Upgrading is a deliberate act by the caller, not a consequence of Stripe deploying.

examples.name: Azure Resource Manager
examples.note: Every request must carry ?api-version= with a dated value; there is no default, so a caller can never drift onto a contract it did not ask for.

examples.name: GitHub REST API
examples.note: A dated request header, X-GitHub-Api-Version, selects the contract, with the media type in Accept still selecting the representation — the two axes kept separate.

async-request-reply.name: Asynchronous Request-Reply
async-request-reply.essence: Accept the work, hand back a handle, and let the caller collect the result later
solves: the load balancer kills the connection before the report finishes rendering
users click submit twice because nothing happened for ninety seconds and the work runs twice
the request thread sits blocked for four minutes doing nothing but waiting
the client has no way to find out whether the import finished or died
a burst of uploads takes the whole web tier down with it

relations.note: A client that never saw the 202 retries the submit, so the accept has to be safe to repeat
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The queue between accept and work is what lets a burst of submissions become depth instead of refusals
relations.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: A large result leaves the status body and becomes a short-lived link the caller fetches
relations.name: Claim Check
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: One operation with one terminal state, rather than a durable multi-step process with compensation
relations.name: Workflow Orchestration
relations.label: Alternative to

themes.name: API Design
themes.role: Answer slow work with a handle instead of a held connection

examples.name: Google Cloud long-running operations
examples.note: A slow method returns an Operation resource instead of a result. It carries done, and then either response or error; callers poll operations.get, and the same shape is reused across services so one client knows how to wait for all of them.

examples.name: Azure Resource Manager async operations
examples.note: Slow control-plane calls answer 202 Accepted with an Azure-AsyncOperation or Operation-Location header naming the status resource, plus Retry-After to set the polling interval.

examples.name: Amazon Textract
examples.note: Document analysis is split in two: a start call returns a JobId, a get call polls it, and completion can also be published to a notification topic so callers can stop polling entirely.

vertical-partitioning.name: Vertical Partitioning
vertical-partitioning.essence: Split an entity by column, so a read touches only the fields it needs
solves: the listing query reads a megabyte per row to display two fields
a stock counter updated on every order keeps invalidating the cached product page
the table has forty columns and the hot query needs three of them
backups are enormous because the database stores images nobody ever queries
only four fields are sensitive but the whole table is under the strict access policy

relations.note: The cold half is often not a table at all: large content moves to object storage and the hot row keeps a reference
relations.name: Object Storage
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Splitting slow-moving fields away from a counter updated on every write is what makes the slow half worth caching
relations.name: In-Process Cache
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Splits the same entity by column instead of splitting the rows across nodes — the other axis of the same decision
relations.name: Sharding
relations.label: Alternative to

themes.name: Performance
themes.role: Stop the hot query paying for columns it never reads

examples.name: Apache Cassandra
examples.note: A table is defined as a set of columns physically grouped and read together, so a query reads only what it names. The split is a layout decision inside one table rather than a second object, which is why the integrity cost of vertical partitioning largely disappears here.

examples.name: Apache HBase
examples.note: Column families are stored in separate files and can be configured independently — different compression, different block size, different in-memory setting — so hot and cold groups of a wide row are tuned separately.

examples.name: PostgreSQL TOAST
examples.note: The engine already does a version of this without being asked: an oversized field is moved out of the main row into a side table and fetched only when the query references it, which is why a wide row can still have a fast index-only scan.

functional-partitioning.name: Functional Partitioning
functional-partitioning.essence: Give each business area its own store, sized and tuned for how that area is used
solves: a monthly report scans the audit tables and checkout slows to a crawl
one database holds four unrelated business areas and is sized for all of them at once
the catalogue wants a search index and the orders want transactions, and they share a server
backups run to the strictest policy any table needs, which costs us for everything
one area of the product needs its data to stay in a region and the query filter keeps being forgotten

relations.note: The context boundary is where the partition should fall, which is what stops the split producing a distributed monolith
relations.name: Bounded Context
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Cross-area events publish from an outbox, so a state change and the event announcing it cannot diverge
relations.name: Outbox
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Once a write can span two stores the transaction is gone, so a compensating sequence takes its place
relations.name: Saga
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Splits the subject rather than the key space — reach for it when areas differ, for sharding when one area is too big
relations.name: Sharding
relations.label: Alternative to

themes.name: Scalability
themes.role: Split by business area so each scales on its own terms

examples.name: Database per service
examples.note: The microservice convention is functional partitioning made a rule: each service owns its own store and no other service reads it directly. It is what makes independent deployment real, and it is why cross-service reads become API calls or maintained views.

examples.name: Amazon service-oriented mandate
examples.note: Amazon is the widely documented early example of forbidding direct access to another team data store and requiring a service interface instead — the organisational rule that makes the functional boundary hold in practice.

examples.name: Regional data residency deployments
examples.note: Regulations that forbid personal data leaving a jurisdiction are commonly satisfied by a store per region rather than a column filter, turning the requirement into topology that cannot be forgotten in a query.

sliding-window.name: Sliding Window
sliding-window.essence: Aggregates the recent past in bounded state, aging events out instead of resetting
solves: my per-minute counter resets on the boundary and lets through double the rate for a moment
I need the count for the last hour, not for the current hour
keeping every event so I can count the recent ones is eating all the memory
the average over the whole day hides the spike that happened ten minutes ago
each fetcher enforces its own limit so the real rate is the limit times the fleet size

relations.note: The window is how the limiter counts — an allowance over any recent minute, not each clock minute
relations.name: Rate Limiter
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Decaying or rotating the sketch's counters is this window applied to an approximate count
relations.name: Count-Min Sketch
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: The aggregator's completion condition is usually a window over arrival time
relations.name: Aggregator
relations.label: Combines with

relations.note: Two shapes of the same allowance: remember arrivals, or refill credit
relations.name: Token Bucket
relations.label: Alternative to

relations.note: The Top-K case study argues true-sliding against tumbling as its Staff-level distinction
relations.name: Top-K
relations.label: Demonstrated by

relations.note: A shared window is what makes a per-domain rate hold across many independent workers
relations.name: Web Crawler
relations.label: Demonstrated by

examples.name: Apache Flink
examples.note: Windowing is a first-class operator over event time or processing time — tumbling, sliding (SlidingEventTimeWindows) and session windows. A watermark decides when a window is complete, and an allowed-lateness setting governs what happens to an event that turns up after its window fired.

examples.name: Kafka Streams
examples.note: Windowed aggregations key a table by window as well as by record key: TimeWindows for tumbling and hopping windows, SessionWindows for activity gaps. Each carries a grace period after which a late record is dropped, and the windowed state store keeps segments only for its configured retention.

examples.name: Redis sorted sets
examples.note: The exact sliding log is built from one sorted set per key: ZADD the arrival timestamp as the score, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to drop everything older than the window, then ZCARD for what remains. The three are usually wrapped in a Lua script so a concurrent request cannot read a half-evicted window.

examples.name: Prometheus
examples.note: A range vector selector such as http_requests_total[5m] takes the samples inside the five minutes ending at the evaluation instant, so a rate() over it is measured back from now rather than over the last whole five-minute block.

god-object.name: God Object
god-object.essence: One class knows and does almost everything
solves: one class knows about everything and every feature has to touch it
unrelated features keep colliding in merge conflicts on the same file
testing this class means mocking half the system
the longest file in the repo grows every sprint and nobody can split it

relations.note: Centralizing coordination, done carefully, avoids one class doing all
relations.name: Mediator
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Injected collaborators keep one class from owning everything
relations.name: Dependency Injection
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: One reason to change keeps a class from swelling into the object that does everything
relations.name: Single Responsibility Principle
relations.label: Mitigated by

spaghetti-code.name: Spaghetti Code
spaghetti-code.essence: Control flow too tangled to follow
solves: changing one thing breaks an unrelated test three modules away
I cannot follow what happens when the button is clicked without a debugger
one function runs hundreds of lines mixing validation, IO and formatting
state is mutated from a dozen far-apart places with no owner

relations.note: Clear tiers keep call flow from tangling
relations.name: Layered / N-Tier
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Keep each concern in its own place and control flow stops threading through everything
relations.name: Separation of Concerns
relations.label: Mitigated by

big-ball-of-mud.name: Big Ball of Mud
solves: there is no layer a change can stay inside
the UI queries the database directly and nothing stops it
anything can import anything and eventually does
the same business rule lives in a controller, a cron job and a database trigger

relations.note: A distributed monolith usually has a tidy diagram — the problem is where the lines fall, not that they are missing.
relations.name: Distributed Monolith
relations.label: Often confused with

relations.note: Isolating the core keeps the mud out
relations.name: Hexagonal
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Enforced layers resist mud
relations.name: Layered / N-Tier
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Replace the mud incrementally instead of a rewrite
relations.name: Strangler Fig
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Boundaries keep models from merging into mud
relations.name: Bounded Context
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Clear concern boundaries are precisely what the mud has dissolved
relations.name: Separation of Concerns
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Deliberate seams are exactly what the mud grew in the absence of
relations.name: Design for Evolution
relations.label: Mitigated by

anemic-domain-model.name: Anemic Domain Model
anemic-domain-model.essence: Data objects with no real behavior of their own
solves: my domain classes are nothing but getters and setters
the same validation rule is copy-pasted across three service classes
any caller can set a total to a negative number and nothing refuses it
business rules live in services while the entities are just data bags

relations.note: Behavior on the aggregate keeps the model rich
relations.name: Aggregate
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Keeping SQL out of the model removes the pressure to flatten it
relations.name: Data Mapper
relations.label: Mitigated by

golden-hammer.name: Golden Hammer
golden-hammer.essence: One familiar tool applied to every problem
solves: we reach for the same tool on every problem without asking whether it fits
we put a message broker between two functions in the same process
a workflow engine drives a single boolean flag
the only answer to why we used this is that it is what we used last time

relations.note: A plug-in per need resists forcing one tool everywhere
relations.name: Microkernel / Plugin
relations.label: Mitigated by

boat-anchor.name: Boat Anchor
boat-anchor.essence: Dead code or hardware kept around unused
solves: nobody can explain what breaks if we delete this module
a server is racked, patched and monitored but has served no traffic for a year
code marked do not remove, may be needed later, with no ticket or owner
a search for callers turns up nothing yet nobody dares delete the file

relations.note: Retire dead legacy slice by slice
relations.name: Strangler Fig
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Build only what is needed now and there is no speculative code left to fossilise
relations.name: You Aren't Gonna Need It (YAGNI)
relations.label: Mitigated by

cache-stampede.name: Cache Stampede
cache-stampede.essence: A popular key expires and a herd of misses hits the source at once
solves: one popular entry expires and hundreds of identical queries hit the database at once
traffic is flat but the database sees a burst of duplicate reads on a regular clock
many requests rebuild the same expensive value in parallel
database load spikes every few minutes matching our expiry time

relations.note: The general form: any crowd released at once, not only cache missers
relations.name: Thundering Herd
relations.label: Often confused with

relations.note: Reload the hot key before its TTL expires, so it never goes cold under load
relations.name: Refresh-Ahead
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: One load path per key lets the cache coalesce concurrent misses into a single fetch
relations.name: Read-Through
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Bound the recomputation to a single in-flight call, so only one miss reaches the source
relations.name: Request Coalescing
relations.label: Mitigated by

hot-key.name: Hot Key
hot-key.essence: One key draws so much traffic it overloads the single node that owns it
solves: one popular record takes millions of reads while every other key sees a handful
adding cache nodes does not help because the traffic all lands on one of them
a single celebrity account overloads the one node that owns it
load is spread evenly except for the one entry everybody wants

relations.note: The storage-tier cousin: a whole shard saturates, not one entry
relations.name: Hot Partition
relations.label: Often confused with

relations.note: Copy the hot entry onto several nodes and spread reads across them
relations.name: Replication
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: A local fallback cache keeps the hottest key in the app's own memory, off the shared node
relations.name: In-Process Cache
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: A key chosen to distribute is a key that never gets hot
relations.name: Partition Around Limits
relations.label: Mitigated by

stale-cache.name: Stale Cache
stale-cache.essence: Reads hit the cache while writes hit the store, so the cache serves old data
solves: users see old data after an update until the entry expires
we write to the database but reads keep serving the previous value
a price change took ten minutes to show up on the site
the cached copy and the source of truth disagree

relations.note: Write the cache and store together, so a read after a write can't be stale
relations.name: Write-Through
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Invalidate the key on write, so the next read reloads the current value
relations.name: Cache-Aside
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Background refresh keeps the entry close to the source, bounding the stale window
relations.name: Refresh-Ahead
relations.label: Mitigated by

race-condition.name: Race Condition
race-condition.essence: Unsynchronized concurrent access whose result depends on timing
solves: intermittent failures we cannot reproduce locally
two people booked the same seat
a counter that should read 1000 reads 847
the tests pass every time and production produces impossible results
flaky behaviour that only shows up under real concurrency

relations.note: Fold the check into the write so the store applies them as one indivisible step
relations.name: Conditional Write
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Attach a version and let a stale write fail, then reload and retry
relations.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Lock the row up front so only the holder can run the check-then-write
relations.name: Pessimistic Locking
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Hold one lock across the check and the write so nothing interleaves
relations.name: Monitor Object
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Exclude everyone during a write; let reads run in parallel the rest of the time
relations.name: Read-Write Lock
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Give one owner the state so there's no sharing to race over at all
relations.name: Thread Confinement
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Serialize per entity rather than detecting the collision afterwards
relations.name: Sequential Convoy
relations.label: Mitigated by

relations.note: Publish a finished copy rather than mutating in place, so no reader can catch a partial write
relations.name: Copy-on-Write
relations.label: Mitigated by

deadlock.name: Deadlock
deadlock.essence: Two holders each wait for a lock the other holds, forever
solves: two transactions each wait on the other and neither ever finishes
the process is stuck with no error, no progress and no timeout
threads park forever and everything behind them piles up
the job hangs indefinitely and only a restart clears it

relations.note: Deadlock halts everyone and is easy to spot; starvation keeps throughput normal and hides
relations.name: Starvation
relations.label: Often confused with

relations.note: One owner per state, coordinating by messages — no shared locks left to form a cycle

tinder.name: Tinder
tinder.essence: Surface nearby profiles in under 300 ms and fire a match the moment two people both swipe right, across billions of swipes a day
solves: two users act on each other at almost the same moment and my check misses that they mutually matched
loading a stack of nearby candidates takes seconds because I scan and filter the whole users table on every request
people keep getting shown profiles they already dismissed and it looks like their actions were lost
I am writing billions of tiny records a day and a single database cannot absorb the volume
one person history of things they have already seen has grown so large that checking against it is slow

relations.note: the candidate stack is a geospatial index query — profiles within N km of the user's current location
relations.name: Geohash
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: an active user's next stack is precomputed by a background job and served straight from cache on app open
relations.name: Materialized View
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: profile edits are streamed into the search index instead of dual-writing, keeping the geo index in sync
relations.name: Change Data Capture
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: Cassandra's log-structured write path absorbs ~2B swipes/day that a B-tree store could not
relations.name: LSM Tree
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the swipe partition key is the sorted user pair, forcing both directions of a pair into one partition for atomic checks
relations.name: Sharding
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the Redis variant combines both ids into one key so a pair's swipes hash to the same shard for an atomic Lua check
relations.name: Consistent Hashing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: heavy swipers get a per-user Bloom filter of their swipe history to keep the already-seen check cheap
relations.name: Bloom Filter
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the last K swipes are cached on the single device and filtered from the next stack, closing the replication-lag window
relations.name: Client-Side Cache
relations.label: Demonstrates

strava.name: Strava
strava.essence: Record a run entirely on the phone, offline, then sync it in one batched upload — the client absorbs the write load so the backend barely sees it
solves: my app has to keep tracking a workout even when the phone has no signal for miles
I ping the server with a GPS point every few seconds and it is melting my backend and the battery
my elapsed-time counter keeps running through pauses so the total time comes out wrong
a year of GPS traces is hundreds of terabytes and one database cannot hold it hot
friends want to watch a workout live but standing up a websocket push tier feels like overkill

relations.note: the phone accepts each GPS write locally and flushes to the system of record only when the activity ends
relations.name: Write-Behind
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a whole activity's ~600-point trace uploads in one request on completion instead of a point every few seconds
relations.name: Batching
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the activity lives in an on-device buffer persisted to local storage, so tracking and live stats never need the network
relations.name: Client-Side Cache
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: active time is derived by summing a STARTED/PAUSED/RESUMED status log rather than mutating an elapsed counter
relations.name: Event Sourcing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the activity store is partitioned by completion time so recent-activity queries hit only a few shards
relations.name: Sharding
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: traces older than a year are tiered off to cheap object storage like S3
relations.name: Object Storage
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the single Activity Service holds no per-request state and scales horizontally under load
relations.name: Stateless Service
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the leaderboard is a precomputed ranking refreshed on a schedule rather than sorted per request
relations.name: Materialized View
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: chunked, background and retried uploads can all deliver the same points twice, so the server dedupes by activity and point and a re-send never double-counts the route
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Demonstrates

whatsapp.name: WhatsApp
whatsapp.essence: Deliver a message in under 500 ms to whoever is online, store it for whoever is not, across billions of persistent connections
solves: a message I send to someone who is offline just disappears instead of arriving when they finally reconnect
chat only works while both people are pinned to the same server, and breaks the moment I add a second machine
polling a REST endpoint for new messages wastes bandwidth and still feels laggy
a phone drops signal and the socket still looks open, so messages vanish with no error
the same conversation shows its messages in a different order on my laptop than on my phone

relations.note: chat servers subscribe to per-user channels so a sender reaches a recipient without knowing which host holds their socket
relations.name: Publish-Subscribe
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: every undelivered message is written to a per-client inbox before delivery, so an offline recipient still receives it on reconnect
relations.name: Inbox
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: an L4 load balancer spreads long-lived WebSocket connections across the chat-server fleet
relations.name: Load Balancer
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a message carries only an attachmentId, keeping large media off the real-time delivery path
relations.name: Claim Check
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: media is uploaded to a dedicated attachment service backed by object storage rather than the message database
relations.name: Object Storage
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: one sent message is delivered to every chat participant and to each of their multiple devices
relations.name: Fan-Out
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: clients ack each push and the server resends until acked, tolerating duplicates so nothing is ever lost
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Demonstrates

fb-live-comments.name: Facebook Live Comments
fb-live-comments.essence: Broadcast thousands of comments a second to millions of live viewers in under 200 ms, favouring availability over consistency
solves: thousands of people are watching the same live stream and every new message has to reach all of them within a fraction of a second
my clients poll for updates every few seconds and it hammers the database with requests that almost always come back empty
a viewer who joins late needs to scroll back through older messages without the pages shifting as new ones keep arriving
one viral broadcast has hundreds of millions of watchers and holding an open connection for each one melts my servers
a phone drops off wifi for ten seconds and the user comes back to a gap in the conversation they cannot recover

relations.note: the Comment Management Service publishes each comment onto a partitioned bus that messaging servers subscribe to per video
relations.name: Publish-Subscribe
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a single posted comment must be delivered to every viewer of that video, from a handful to hundreds of millions
relations.name: Fan-Out
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the L7 load balancer hashes on liveVideoId so same-video viewers converge on the same messaging server, keeping subscription sets small
relations.name: Consistent Hashing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a Layer 7 load balancer inspects the request and routes by liveVideoId rather than blindly round-robining connections
relations.name: Load Balancer
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: mega-streams snapshot recent comments to the edge every second and clients poll the CDN instead of holding a live push connection
relations.name: CDN
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: recent comments live in a shared Redis cache so any messaging server can replay them when a reconnecting viewer lands elsewhere
relations.name: Distributed Cache
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: on reconnect the same comment can arrive via both SSE replay and the live stream, so the client dedupes by comment id
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Demonstrates

google-docs.name: Google Docs
google-docs.essence: A hundred people edit one document at once and every screen converges on the same text within 100 ms
solves: two people type into the same document at the same time and one persons edits silently overwrite the others
edits arrive in a different order on each screen so everyone ends up staring at a slightly different version of the text
I want a collaborators keystrokes and cursor to show up on my screen in well under a tenth of a second
one real-time server holds the sockets for every open document and tips over past a few thousand users
the edit history for a hot document grows without bound and replaying it to each new joiner takes seconds

relations.note: the append-only operation log is the source of truth and the visible text is a projection replayed from it
relations.name: Event Sourcing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a user's own keystroke is applied to their local view before any server round trip, then reconciled via transform when the authoritative order arrives
relations.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: once an edit is ordered and logged, the owning server broadcasts it to every other socket on that document
relations.name: Fan-Out
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: documents are assigned to owning Document Service instances via a ZooKeeper-backed hash ring so adding or removing a server reshuffles only a slice
relations.name: Consistent Hashing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: every WebSocket for one document is pinned to the single server that owns and orders that document
relations.name: Sticky Session
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: compaction collapses a document's long operation history into a precomputed snapshot under a new version marker
relations.name: Materialized View
relations.label: Demonstrates

online-chess.name: Online Chess
online-chess.essence: Match players by rating, run 500K real-time games where the server owns every board and clock, and rank 10M players live
solves: two workers both claim the same waiting player and double-book them into two matches
keeping live session state in a shared store makes every action pay a network round trip
a server that holds in-memory sessions crashes and takes every one of them down with it
a distant player keeps losing on the clock because their own network lag comes out of their own time
showing someone their exact rank means counting millions of rows above them on every request

relations.note: each live game is owned by one server that holds its board and clocks in memory and processes its own moves serially
relations.name: Actor Model
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: gameId is mapped to a game server through a hash ring plus a membership registry so both players land together and node changes remap only a slice
relations.name: Consistent Hashing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: every accepted move is appended to a durable log before it is broadcast, so a crash can never leave players ahead of the record
relations.name: Write-Ahead Log
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a replacement server rebuilds the board by replaying the move log, and a rating is a fold over finished games rather than a stored value
relations.name: Event Sourcing
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: two matchers racing for the same waiting player are resolved by an atomic ZREM claim where exactly one wins and losers retry, no lock held
relations.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a generation counter on the game row guards every write with WHERE generation <= :gen, so a partitioned zombie server's stale updates are silently dropped
relations.name: Conditional Write
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: exact rank is served from a Redis sorted set derived from finished games, never the source of truth and always rebuildable by reconciliation
relations.name: Materialized View
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the worker that claims a player publishes matchFound on a channel keyed by requestId to whichever node holds that player's long-poll
relations.name: Publish-Subscribe
relations.label: Demonstrates

leetcode.name: LeetCode
leetcode.essence: Run untrusted user code safely in under 5 seconds, and keep a 100k-user contest leaderboard live
solves: I have to run code that strangers submit without it deleting my data or mining crypto on my servers
one submission with an infinite loop pins the CPU and takes every other in-flight request down with it
recomputing a live leaderboard by scanning and sorting the whole submissions table on every poll is crushing my database
a burst of submissions during a contest overwhelms my workers and requests start timing out
spinning up a fresh sandbox for every job is too slow to hit my latency budget

relations.note: warm language containers are kept ready and reused across submissions instead of cold-starting one per job
relations.name: Object Pool
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a worker fleet pulls submissions off the queue, each grabbing the next job as its capacity frees up
relations.name: Competing Consumers
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the submission queue absorbs a contest's spike and drains it at the fleet's sustainable rate
relations.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: each language-specific container pool grows and shrinks on CPU utilization to track contest load
relations.name: Autoscaling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the live leaderboard is a Redis sorted set updated on each accepted submission, not recomputed per poll
relations.name: Materialized View
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the sandbox is stripped to a read-only filesystem, no network, capped CPU/memory, and a seccomp syscall whitelist
relations.name: Least Privilege
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: each submission runs in its own disposable container so a crash or hang can't take the API server or other jobs down
relations.name: Bulkhead
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a hard per-test-case timeout kills a runaway or infinite-loop submission and keeps grading inside the ~5-second result target
relations.name: Timeout / Deadline
relations.label: Demonstrates

dropbox.name: Dropbox
dropbox.essence: Store, share, and sync files up to 50GB by moving bytes directly between client and blob storage — the app server signs URLs but never touches the data
solves: I need users to upload huge files but a single request times out and my API gateway caps the body size
my users lose the whole upload when their connection drops halfway and have to start over from scratch
downloads are painfully slow for users far from my one data center
listing every file shared with a given user means scanning the permission list of every file I store
an edit made on a laptop should appear on the phone within seconds without anyone pressing refresh

relations.note: the File Service hands the client a presigned URL — a signed, time-limited grant to write to or read from one exact blob location

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: file bytes live in an S3-style blob store, not on the app servers or in the metadata database
relations.name: Object Storage
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: downloads are served from the edge cache nearest the user, with only a miss reaching origin blob storage
relations.name: CDN
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: an LB and API gateway front the File Service, handling routing, TLS termination, rate limiting, and request validation
relations.name: API Gateway
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the File Service signs URLs locally and holds no per-request state, so it scales out horizontally behind the load balancer
relations.name: Stateless Service
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the server publishes file change events over a persistent per-device connection so edits propagate to other devices in real time
relations.name: Publish-Subscribe
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: resumable chunked uploads rely on re-reported or re-uploaded chunks being safe no-ops, with a content fingerprint deduplicating identical uploads
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: signed URLs are scoped to one object and expire in minutes, optionally bound to an IP or auth cookie, granting the narrowest access for the shortest time
relations.name: Least Privilege
relations.label: Demonstrates

youtube.name: YouTube
youtube.essence: Take a 10-GB upload straight to blob storage, transcode it into segments, and stream it worldwide with adaptive bitrate
solves: users upload multi-gigabyte files and my app servers fall over trying to proxy every byte
a viewer on a spotty connection keeps buffering because I only stored one giant video file
when an upload drops at 90% the user has to start the whole thing over from scratch
one clip goes viral and the single database node holding its record melts under the read load
transcoding a long video into every device format takes forever on a single machine

relations.note: the Video Service hands the client a presigned URL so multi-gigabyte bytes upload straight to the blob store, never through the app tier
relations.name: Valet Key
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: segments, renditions, and manifests all live in an S3-style blob store — the only tier that scales to a petabyte of new video a day

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: post-processing is a pipeline of split then transcode then manifest-generation, each a discrete transform over the previous stage's output
relations.name: Pipe-and-Filter
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a Temporal-style orchestrator builds the processing DAG and schedules worker nodes at the right time
relations.name: Workflow Orchestration
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: independent segments are transcoded in parallel by a fleet of interchangeable workers pulling from a queue
relations.name: Competing Consumers
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a distributed cache keyed by videoId absorbs reads for popular videos so they never reach Cassandra
relations.name: Cache-Aside
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: segments and manifests are pushed to edge servers so streaming never travels back to the origin region
relations.name: CDN
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: hot video metadata is replicated onto extra Cassandra nodes so several can share a viral clip's read load
relations.name: Replication
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the Video Service keeps no per-request state, so it scales out horizontally behind the load balancer
relations.name: Stateless Service
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: The assembled-upload event is an idempotent trigger, so a retried notification cannot start the pipeline twice
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: A sweep over rows stuck in Processing past a threshold closes the gap an unowned event source leaves
relations.name: Sweeper
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: Queue messages carry blob-store URLs, not video bytes — the broker never needs the store's bandwidth budget

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: The queue in front of the workers lets the fleet run near the daily mean instead of the peak
relations.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: A file that crashes the encoder comes back forever; bounded attempts route it out, marking the video Failed with a reason
relations.name: Dead Letter Channel
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: VideoMetadata partitions by video id so metadata scales independently of the blob tier
relations.name: Sharding
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: Popular rows get a shared cache in front of the metadata store, stacked with a higher replication factor
relations.name: Distributed Cache
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: One entry point terminates TLS, authenticates uploaders and applies per-account limits
relations.name: API Gateway
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: Workers scale on queue depth and oldest-message age — a transcode fleet runs at 100% CPU by definition, so utilisation never fires
relations.name: Autoscaling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: View counts tally in memory and flush an atomic add every few seconds, turning 1,200 increments into one write
relations.name: Write-Behind
relations.label: Demonstrates

chatgpt.name: ChatGPT
chatgpt.essence: Stream an LLM's answer token-by-token to 200M users while fairly scheduling a scarce pool of GPUs
solves: my users stare at a blank screen for thirty seconds while the backend computes the whole answer before sending anything
a burst of requests slams my expensive workers all at once and latency spirals instead of degrading gracefully
one heavy user drains my scarce pool of accelerators and everyone else's requests starve
replaying the entire conversation into the model on every turn keeps getting slower and more expensive
a routine deploy kills thousands of in-flight streaming responses mid-sentence

relations.note: a request queue sits between bursty prompts (~20k/s) and fixed-rate GPU workers, absorbing spikes as bounded wait instead of dropped requests
relations.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a pool of GPU workers pulls generation jobs off one shared queue whenever a worker has free capacity
relations.name: Competing Consumers
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the generation queue is bounded with an admission policy that sheds or defers once too deep, which also bounds an admitted request's wait time
relations.name: Backpressure
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: continuous batching advances dozens of sequences per GPU forward pass, the single biggest lever on utilization of memory-bandwidth-bound hardware
relations.name: Batching
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: workers publish token deltas on a per-runId channel that whichever instance holds the client's SSE connection subscribes to and relays
relations.name: Publish-Subscribe
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a runId minted at generation start lets a worker and the connection-holding instance rendezvous without direct knowledge, and lets a reconnecting client resume the right stream
relations.name: Correlation Identifier
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: cost-aware per-user token budgets that refill over time, plus tier-weighted queueing, meter actual GPU scarcity instead of raw request counts
relations.name: Rate Limiter
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the Chat Service holds no per-request state, so any instance can serve, relay, or resume a stream and the tier redeploys and scales freely
relations.name: Stateless Service
relations.label: Demonstrates

ticketmaster.name: Ticketmaster
ticketmaster.essence: Hold a seat while a fan checks out, never sell it twice, and keep the event page fast when ten million refresh at once
solves: two customers both paid for the same seat because each checkout thought it was free
a fan fills out a five-minute payment form only to find the seat is already gone
my event page melts the instant tickets go on sale and millions hit refresh at once
how do I let someone hold an item during checkout and automatically release it if they walk away

relations.note: the DB confirm is guarded by an OCC check so only one buyer wins a contested seat even after the lock lapses
relations.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the Stripe webhook handler dedupes on booking ID because Stripe retries deliveries
relations.name: Idempotency
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: event, performer, and static venue data are served from a read-through cache so the read burst rarely reaches Postgres
relations.name: Read-Through
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: a virtual waiting queue admits fans in controlled batches, smoothing the on-sale spike before it reaches booking
relations.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: Postgres inserts, updates, and deletes stream to Elasticsearch to keep the search index fresh
relations.name: Change Data Capture
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: non-personalised search results are pushed to the edge so identical queries never hit the origin
relations.name: CDN
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: one gateway fronts auth, rate limiting, and routing to the event, search, and booking services
relations.name: API Gateway
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the Event Service holds no per-request state, so it scales horizontally behind a load balancer during the stampede
relations.name: Stateless Service
relations.label: Demonstrates

online-auction.name: Online Auction
online-auction.essence: Hold one true highest bid under a storm of concurrent bids, lose none, and broadcast each new high in real time
solves: two people submit at the same instant and both get told they are winning because each read a stale current value
under a last-minute traffic spike my service either drops writes or falls over, and I cannot afford to lose a single one
my clients poll every few seconds for the latest number and still act on stale data while hammering the database
one user is on server A and another on server B watching the same item, and an update on A never reaches B live connections
I overwrite the current maximum on every update and now I have no history left to settle a dispute

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the winning update lands only WHERE max_bid still equals the value just read, closing the read-then-write race on the high bid

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: every bid is appended to a partitioned Kafka topic and acknowledged before adjudication, so no bid is lost to a crash
relations.name: Message Queue
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the queue absorbs an auction's final-minute bid surge so the Bid Service consumes at a steady rate instead of being over-provisioned
relations.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: an accepted high is published to a per-auction channel so every SSE server, not just the one that judged it, learns the new number
relations.name: Publish-Subscribe
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: each SSE server pushes the new high to all of its own connected watchers of that auction
relations.name: Fan-Out
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the auction store is partitioned by auctionId so ~15k writes/sec spread across instances with no cross-shard reads
relations.name: Sharding
relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the Bid and Auction services hold no per-request state, so an autoscaler can add instances freely under bursty load
relations.name: Stateless Service

robinhood.name: Robinhood

a confirmation comes back keyed by the vendor id, but my database is sharded by user so I cannot find the row to update
an order reached the exchange but the write that followed failed, and now my records disagree with reality
order placement has to finish in under 200 ms even when everyone trades at the opening bell

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: all exchange-bound order traffic is funnelled through one dispatch gateway with a small fixed egress

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.note: the order store is horizontally partitioned by userId so a user's orders and queries live on one node

relations.label: Demonstrates

relations.label: Demonstrates
